```{r setup}
library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(classInt)
library(spdep)

# Data written by data-raw/get_data.R (copies of what the practicals download live)
backup <- "../data/backup/"
read_wkt <- function(file, crs) st_as_sf(read.csv(file), wkt = "geometry", crs = crs)

study_wards <- read_wkt(paste0(backup, "leeds_wards.csv"), 4326) |>
  filter(WD26NM %in% c("Little London & Woodhouse", "Hunslet & Riverside", "Headingley & Hyde Park")) |>
  st_transform(27700)
study_area <- st_union(study_wards)

leeds_lsoa <- read_wkt(paste0(backup, "leeds_lsoa.csv"), 4326) |> st_transform(27700)
study_lsoa <- leeds_lsoa[lengths(st_intersects(st_point_on_surface(st_geometry(leeds_lsoa)), study_area)) > 0, ]

population <- read.csv(paste0(backup, "leeds_lsoa_population.csv"))
names(population) <- toupper(names(population))
workplace <- read.csv(paste0(backup, "leeds_lsoa_workplace.csv")) |> select(LSOA21CD, workplace)

crimes <- bind_rows(read.csv(paste0(backup, "crimes_2026-07.csv")),
                    read.csv(paste0(backup, "crimes_2026-08.csv"))) |>
  select(id, category, month, location.street.name, location.longitude, location.latitude) |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("location.longitude", "location.latitude"), crs = 4326) |>
  st_transform(27700) |>
  st_filter(study_area)
august <- filter(crimes, month == "2026-08")
burglary <- filter(crimes, category == "burglary")   # July and August

streets <- read_wkt("../data/leeds_streets.csv", 27700)

study_lsoa <- study_lsoa |>
  mutate(crimes = lengths(st_intersects(study_lsoa, august))) |>
  left_join(population, by = c("LSOA21CD" = "GEOGRAPHY_CODE")) |>
  left_join(workplace, by = "LSOA21CD") |>
  mutate(rate = crimes / OBS_VALUE * 1000,
         rate_wp = crimes / workplace * 1000)

theme_set(theme_void(base_size = 16))
purple <- "#5b2a86"
```

# Talk 1: What is place? {background-color="#5b2a86"}

## {.mm-slide}

::: {.mm}
"We are too far along in the scientific study of crime and place to leave unit of analysis to the serendipitous interest of singular scholars." (Weisburd, Bruinsma & Bernasco, 2009, p. 5)
:::

## What, where … and why?

- Criminology of place: crime is concentrated at **micro-places** (street segments, hot spots).
- Strong on **what** happens **where**.
- Weaker on **why** (Bannister, O'Sullivan & Bates, 2019).
- Places have histories, uses, meanings, and they change over **time**.


## Spatial data = attributes + location

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
The **vector** data model:

- **Points**: a crime, a pub, a bus stop
- **Lines**: a street, a river, a bus route
- **Polygons**: a ward, an LSOA, a police neighbourhood

Plus **raster**: a grid of cells, such as a density surface.

In R, `sf` stores vector data as a **table with a geometry column**.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r vector-types, fig.width=6, fig.height=6}
one_ward <- filter(study_wards, WD26NM == "Little London & Woodhouse")
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = one_ward, fill = "#efe7f6", colour = purple, linewidth = 1) +
  geom_sf(data = st_intersection(streets, st_geometry(one_ward)), colour = "grey45", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_sf(data = st_filter(august, one_ward), colour = "#d7301f", size = 1, alpha = 0.6) +
  labs(caption = "Polygon: Little London & Woodhouse ward.\nLines: its streets. Points: its crimes, August 2026.")
```
:::
::::


## What is a neighbourhood?

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}
- No agreed definition (Galster, 2001). Residents, police and statisticians all draw different lines.
- We often fall back on **administrative units**: LSOAs (~1,500 residents), wards (~25,000).
- Or go smaller: the **street segment** (Weisburd et al., 2012).
- Same crimes, different units, different story.
:::

::: {.column width="60%"}
```{r units, fig.width=8, fig.height=5}
ward_counts <- study_wards |> mutate(crimes = lengths(st_intersects(study_wards, august)))
two <- bind_rows(
  study_lsoa |> transmute(unit = paste(nrow(study_lsoa), "LSOAs"), crimes),
  ward_counts |> transmute(unit = "3 wards", crimes))
ggplot(two) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = crimes), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  facet_wrap(~ unit) +
  scale_fill_distiller(palette = "RdPu", direction = 1, trans = "sqrt", name = "Crimes") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```
:::
::::

## The data are already a representation

```{r snap}
top_snap <- august |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  count(location.street.name, sort = TRUE) |>
  slice(1)
n_points <- nrow(distinct(as.data.frame(st_coordinates(august))))
```

- police.uk moves each crime to the nearest of a fixed set of **snap points**, to protect victims.
- In August 2026, `r nrow(august)` crimes in our three Leeds wards sit on just **`r n_points` distinct points**.
- Crime data record only what is **reported and recorded**.

➜ **Practical 0** (if new to R) and **Part 1**

# Talk 2: Maps as arguments {background-color="#5b2a86"}

## {.mm-slide}

::: {.mm}
"Making sensible judgments about how you represent your data … will help your web map tell the right story." Field (2012)
:::

## Reference and thematic maps

- **Reference maps** show where things are: streets, rivers, boundaries.
- **Thematic maps** show how something varies across space: crime, rates, populations.
- A good crime map is a thematic layer on a light reference base, with a clear **visual hierarchy**.
- Every map someone else reads needs: title, legend, scale, **sources**.

## Counts or rates? The denominator dilemma

```{r rates, fig.width=12, fig.height=4.8}
two_maps <- bind_rows(
  study_lsoa |> mutate(measure = "Count", value = crimes),
  study_lsoa |> mutate(measure = "Per 1,000 residents", value = rate),
  study_lsoa |> mutate(measure = "Per 1,000 workplace population", value = rate_wp)) |>
  mutate(measure = factor(measure, levels = unique(measure))) |>
  group_by(measure) |> mutate(quintile = factor(ntile(value, 5))) |> ungroup()
ggplot(two_maps) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = quintile), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  facet_wrap(~ measure) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "RdPu", name = "Quintile")
```

Who is "at risk"? Residents, workers, shoppers, homes, cars…? The city centre has few residents but many workers. Workplace population: Census 2021, table WP001.

## Same data, three classifications

```{r classes, fig.width=12, fig.height=4.8}
shade_by <- function(x, style) {
  as.integer(cut(x, unique(classIntervals(x, n = 5, style = style)$brks), include.lowest = TRUE))
}
classified <- bind_rows(
  study_lsoa |> mutate(method = "Equal interval", class = shade_by(rate, "equal")),
  study_lsoa |> mutate(method = "Quantile", class = shade_by(rate, "quantile")),
  study_lsoa |> mutate(method = "Natural breaks (Jenks)", class = shade_by(rate, "jenks")))
ggplot(classified) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = factor(class)), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  facet_wrap(~ method) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "RdPu", name = "Class\n(1 = lowest)")
```

Crimes per 1,000 residents, August 2026. Calm or alarming? It depends on the break points.

## Where the breaks fall

```{r class-breaks, fig.width=12, fig.height=6}
methods <- c("Equal interval" = "equal", "Quantile" = "quantile", "Natural breaks (Jenks)" = "jenks")
break_lines <- bind_rows(lapply(names(methods), function(m)
  data.frame(method = m, brk = classIntervals(study_lsoa$rate, n = 5, style = methods[[m]])$brks)))
ggplot(classified, aes(rate, fill = factor(class))) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, colour = "grey60", linewidth = 0.2) +
  geom_vline(data = break_lines, aes(xintercept = brk), colour = "grey20", linewidth = 0.6) +
  facet_wrap(~ method, ncol = 1) +
  # scale_x_sqrt() +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "RdPu", name = "Class\n(1 = lowest)") +
  labs(x = "Crimes per 1,000 residents", y = "Number of LSOAs") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 16)
```

## Colour

- **Sequential**: low to high (counts, rates).
- **Diverging**: above and below a meaningful middle (e.g. the average).
- **Qualitative**: categories without order (crime types).
- Colour-blind safe. Survives black-and-white printing. No rainbows for ordered data.
- ColorBrewer (Brewer) and viridis palettes are designed for this.

➜ **Part 2**

# Talk 3: Near and far {background-color="#5b2a86"}

## {.mm-slide}

::: {.mm}
"Everything is related to everything else, but near things are more related than distant things." Tobler (1970)
:::

## Tobler's first law of geography

- **Spatial autocorrelation**: the correlation among values that comes from their relative location.
- **Positive**: neighbours are alike (high next to high). Usual for crime.
- **Negative**: neighbours are unlike, like a chessboard. Rare.
- It matters **substantively** (clustering, spillover, shared causes) and **statistically** (observations are not independent).

## What is a neighbour?

```{r neighbours, fig.width=11, fig.height=5.2}
grid5 <- st_make_grid(st_as_sfc(st_bbox(c(xmin = 0, ymin = 0, xmax = 5, ymax = 5))), n = c(5, 5)) |> st_sf()
centre <- 13
label_nb <- function(nb, criterion) {
  grid5 |> mutate(criterion = criterion,
                  contiguity = case_when(row_number() == centre ~ "Area itself",
                                         row_number() %in% nb[[centre]] ~ "First order",
                                         row_number() %in% nblag(nb, 2)[[2]][[centre]] ~ "Second order",
                                         TRUE ~ "Not a neighbour"))
}
bind_rows(label_nb(poly2nb(grid5, queen = FALSE), "Rook: shares an edge"),
          label_nb(poly2nb(grid5, queen = TRUE), "Queen: shares an edge or a corner")) |>
  mutate(contiguity = factor(contiguity, levels = c("Area itself", "First order", "Second order", "Not a neighbour"))) |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = contiguity), colour = "black") +
  facet_wrap(~ criterion) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Area itself" = "#b2df8a", "First order" = "#1f78b4",
                               "Second order" = "#a6cee3", "Not a neighbour" = "white"), name = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", strip.text = element_text(size = 16))
```

Contiguity (rook, queen, and its order) is the most common definition. Others: distance (within 500 m, the 5 nearest), travel time, flows of people.

## The spatial weights matrix

```{r toy}
toy <- st_make_grid(st_as_sfc(st_bbox(c(xmin = 0, ymin = 0, xmax = 3, ymax = 2))), n = c(3, 2)) |> st_sf()
toy$id <- c("D", "E", "F", "A", "B", "C")   # the grid starts bottom left, so label the top row A-C
nb_toy <- poly2nb(toy, queen = FALSE)
abc <- order(toy$id)
w_b <- nb2mat(nb_toy, style = "B"); dimnames(w_b) <- list(toy$id, toy$id); w_b <- w_b[abc, abc]
w_w <- nb2mat(nb_toy, style = "W"); dimnames(w_w) <- list(toy$id, toy$id); w_w <- w_w[abc, abc]
```

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="24%"}
```{r toy-map, fig.width=3, fig.height=2.4}
ggplot(toy) +
  geom_sf(fill = "#efe7f6", colour = purple, linewidth = 1) +
  geom_sf_text(aes(label = id), size = 9, colour = purple)
```
Rook neighbours
:::

::: {.column width="38%"}
**Binary** (`style = "B"`)

```{r toy-b}
knitr::kable(w_b)
```
1 = neighbour. Symmetrical. Rows sum to the number of neighbours.
:::

::: {.column width="38%"}
**Row-standardised** (`style = "W"`)

```{r toy-w}
knitr::kable(round(w_w, 2))
```
Each row sums to 1: the **average** of the neighbours. Not symmetrical.
:::
::::

## Neighbours in our LSOAs

```{r lsoa-nb}
nb_lsoa <- poly2nb(study_lsoa, queen = TRUE)
lsoa_centres <- st_point_on_surface(st_geometry(study_lsoa))
links <- nb2lines(nb_lsoa, coords = lsoa_centres, as_sf = TRUE)
```

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="35%"}
- Queen contiguity, `r nrow(study_lsoa)` LSOAs.
- `r sum(card(nb_lsoa))` links: on average `r round(mean(card(nb_lsoa)), 1)` neighbours each.
- Each line joins the centres of two LSOAs that touch.
- **Edge effect**: LSOAs at the boundary lose their neighbours outside the study area.
:::

::: {.column width="65%"}
```{r lsoa-nb-map, fig.width=7, fig.height=6}
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = study_lsoa, fill = "grey95", colour = "grey60") +
  geom_sf(data = links, colour = "#d7301f", linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_sf(data = lsoa_centres, size = 1.2)
```
:::
::::

## From neighbours to Moran's I

```{r moran}
study_lsoa$burglary <- lengths(st_intersects(study_lsoa, burglary))
w_lsoa <- nb2listw(nb_lsoa, style = "W")
study_lsoa$burglary_lag <- lag.listw(w_lsoa, study_lsoa$burglary)
set.seed(2026)
mt <- moran.mc(study_lsoa$burglary, w_lsoa, nsim = 999)
```

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
- **Spatial lag**: the average value of an area's neighbours (row-standardised weights × values).
- **Moran's I**: how strongly values go with their spatial lag.
- Burglary per LSOA, July–August 2026: **I = `r round(mt$statistic, 2)`**, p = `r round(mt$p.value, 3)` (999 random shuffles).
- Global: *how much* clustering, not *where*.
:::

::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r moran-plot, fig.width=6, fig.height=5}
ggplot(st_drop_geometry(study_lsoa), aes(burglary, burglary_lag)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7, size = 2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, colour = "#d7301f") +
  labs(x = "Burglaries in the LSOA", y = "Average in its neighbours") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 16)
```
:::
::::

## Why it matters: regression

- Regression assumes **independent** observations. Neighbouring areas are not.
- Ignore it: standard errors too small, effects "significant" that aren't.
- Check: map the model's **residuals**, and test them with Moran's I using the same weights.
- If needed: **spatial lag** and **spatial error** models build $W$ into the model.
- Every result rests on the decision: who is a neighbour, and how much do they count?
